extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing flash-fiction writers and literary-magazine contributors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing flash (short-short) fiction pieces—craft, structure, and marketing—for works typically up to ~1,000 words, with notes on micro/hint fiction and publication avenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-count definitions and ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction will likely clock in at five hundred to one thousand words although lengths are open to debate. Hint fiction and micro-fiction can be a mere twenty-five to one hundred words and should perhaps be considered a separate genre from flash fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these ranges as general guidelines rather than strict rules; recognize related forms (hint/micro-fiction) may require different techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity does not imply a 'small' idea
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important that you not consider brevity a signal to use a 'small' idea for your story. Don’t fall into the trap of saving your 'big' or 'important' stories for longer projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most story ideas boil down to the same handful of conflicts and universal truths; a sound idea can be explored deeply even in a short form and later refined for other projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every word must be essential / economy of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Like a poem, a flash fiction relies on every word being essential. There is no room for multiple plot lines, minor characters, superfluous descriptive passages, or dialogue that does not drive the storyline or give readers a deeper insight into your characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the piece with tight editing — eliminate anything that doesn't advance plot, theme, or character insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain beginning–middle–end structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning-middle-end structure remains the framework for a satisfying story, even those presented with an economy of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in very short pieces ensure setup, development (conflict escalation or complication), and payoff/resolution (explicit or ironic) are present or clearly implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: One plot / one conflict rule of thumb
rubrics_metrics.description: One plot and one conflict should be your rule of thumb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid multiple plot lines or secondary conflicts that dilute the limited space; focus the narrative on a central problem or tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening must grab the reader immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Like any good piece of writing your opening must grab your readers by the throat and not let go. In flash fiction particularly, there is no room for unnecessary setting up. Drop your readers right into the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a setting, action, or line of conversation that raises immediate questions or stakes so readers want to continue; the example from Joyce Carol Oates shows starting in medias res to provoke curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of tense and point of view matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of tense and point of view can be essential in flash fiction since some elements of development are more implicit than explicit given the economy of words necessary in the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past tense can allow events to unfold more quickly; present tense may read differently. Third-person may allow more character development with fewer words than a constrained first-person. Rewriting in different tenses/voices is recommended to find the most effective version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle: imply development and escalate obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Your middle has the same job in flash fiction as it does in a three-hundred-page novel. This is where you set up and develop the conflict facing your protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escalate the protagonist’s obstacles (even if implied) and show forces arrayed against them; implication and suggestion are valuable in flash to convey development without lengthy exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payoff: deliver a strong, often ironic, ending
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful flash fiction will have a kick-butt ending for your readers. The ironic twists of O. Henry and the often-heartbreaking climax resolutions of episodes of Rod Serling’s Twilight Zone are fine templates for the types of endings that make flash fiction work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider starting from an ironic twist and working toward it; endings should resonate emotionally or intellectually and feel earned even if compressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and cultural touchstones as anchors
rubrics_metrics.description: Using well-known models (Hemingway’s six-word story myth, O. Henry twists, Twilight Zone climaxes, law-based conceits like the tattoo example) can provide structural or thematic inspiration for a flash piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor the story in a vivid, recognizable conceit or constraint that generates conflict or irony, then pare it down to essential elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite and experiment with form
rubrics_metrics.description: A benefit of flash fiction is that you can expediently rewrite your piece in a different tense or a different narrative voice and look at them side by side. This might be a daunting task when writing a novel but should be part of your regular flash fiction writing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat flash pieces as iterative: try alternate POVs, tenses, and cuts to find the tightest and most effective version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing and publication strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional-length short stories still dominate printed literary magazines and journals, but online publications offer a seemingly endless stream of opportunities for placing flash fictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research markets by reading outlets for compatibility, submit to online journals and lit mags you’ve read, and promote work via open mics, libraries, bookstores, author appearances, and performance venues to cultivate readers and new audiences.
